reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Michael put on his coat all by himself. The zipper was hard. He pulled and pulled. Then the zipper went up. His teacher smiled. "Nice work, Michael," she said.

At school, Michael saw his friend Sam. Sam's shoes were on the wrong feet. Sam looked shy. He hid his feet under the rug. "I can't do the buckle," Sam said.

Michael sat down next to Sam. "Watch me," he said. Michael pulled the strap. He pushed the buckle. Click. The buckle was on. Sam tried the other shoe. He pulled the strap. He pushed the buckle. It did not click.

"Try again," said Michael. Sam pulled the strap slow this time. He pushed the buckle. Click. Sam jumped up. "I did it." Both shoes were on the right feet now.

The class went to wash hands for snack time. The soap smelled like lemons. Michael sniffed his hands. "Mmm," he said. Sam sniffed too. After snack, the class napped on little mats. Then they went outside to play.

At pick-up time, Michael's mom came. She pointed at his coat. "Who zipped that?" she asked. Michael puffed out his chest. "Me," he said. Then he bent down and buckled his shoes again, just to show her.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Baby Mia was crying in the basket. She was little and red in the face. Lincoln wanted her to stop.

Mama said, "She may be cold." Lincoln touched Mia's tiny hand. It felt cool, like a small stone.

"I will fetch her blanket," Lincoln said. He ran to his bed. He grabbed his soft blue blanket. It smelled like sleep and warm milk. He laid it over Mia, very gently.

Mia stopped crying. She opened her eyes. She made a small sound, like a duck.

"She is warm now," said Mama.

Mia wrapped her hand around Lincoln's finger. Her hand was warm now too.

"You are not alone, Mia," Lincoln said. "I am here."

Mia yawned. Then she fell asleep under the blue blanket.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Charlie went to the basketball court with her dad. The sun made a long shadow by the net. Charlie held a red beanbag in her hands. She wanted to throw it into the hoop.

"Throw it high," said Dad. "One, two, three, up!" Charlie threw it. The beanbag hit the rim and fell down. She tried again. "One, two, three, up!" This time it went in. The net moved and made a soft swish. Charlie clapped her hands.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. The ball bounced off her arms. It rolled a long way across the court. Charlie ran after it and patted it, like patting a sleepy cat. "Nice pat," said Dad. "Now make your arms into a big bowl." Charlie held out both arms. "One, two, three, catch!" The ball landed right in them and stuck, like a magnet on the fridge.

Dad smiled and held up the beanbag. "Want to try both together?" Charlie nodded. She threw the beanbag into the hoop. Then she held out her arms. The big ball came, and she caught it. "I did both!" said Charlie. Dad picked her up and spun her around, and the net above them went swish, swish, swish.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Lincoln ran to the school garden. Today was planting day! He held three little seeds in his hand.

"I will plant a carrot," he said. His teacher, Miss Ana, helped him dig a small hole. Lincoln dropped the seed in. He patted the dirt down. Then he watered it with a tiny blue can.

Every day Lincoln ran to look. One morning, a green sprout peeked out! Lincoln jumped up and down. But next to it, nothing grew. That spot had no sprout at all. It was a puzzle.

"Why did this one grow?" Lincoln asked. He looked and looked. Then he saw it. The empty spot was dry and cracked. His sprout had wet, dark dirt. He had poured water there every day. The water made the seed grow.

"Maybe more water will help!" Lincoln said. He gave the dry spot a big drink. He waited and waited.

Days later, a tiny sprout popped up there too. "It worked!" Lincoln cheered.

At last, a fat orange carrot grew. Miss Ana washed it at the sink. She cut it into round little coins. Lincoln took a bite. It was not salty. It was sweet and crunchy. Lincoln smiled. "Water next, then carrots," he said. "Every time!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was on the table. Nora wanted the crunchy carrots right now. Grandma said, "First we wash hands." Nora looked at her hands. They had dirt on them from the garden. She did not want to wait.

Grandma helped her at the sink. Grandma made the water warm. Nora rubbed the soap all over. "Now we sing the hand song," said Grandma. They sang it all the way through. The bubbles went down the drain. Nora looked at her hands. The dirt was gone. The soap made the dirt go away.

Nora marched to the table. She picked up a carrot. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "Yum," said Nora. Grandma smiled. "More carrots?" she asked. "Yes please," was Nora's answer.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Emmett wanted a snack before his nap. Mom was baking bread in the kitchen. Emmett used his nose to sniff the air. "Mmm, it smells sweet," he said. "What is that smell?" He answered himself: "Bread!"

He used his ears to listen. He heard a bump, bump, bump. "What is that sound?" he asked. Mom laughed. "That is the dough in the bowl. It is rising like a balloon." Emmett touched the bowl with one finger. It felt soft and warm, like a cat's tummy.

"I want to taste it," said Emmett. "Not yet," said Mom. "It is still warm from the oven." She gave him a little crust on a plate. Emmett used his eyes to look at it. It was brown and bumpy. He took a big bite. "Crunch!" he said. "My ears hear my own snack!"

Emmett helped Mom sweep the crumbs off the table. "One crumb, two crumbs, three crumbs," he counted. Then he patted his tummy. "My tummy says thank you." Mom kissed his wild, messy hair. "Nap time now, bread boy." Emmett yawned and hugged his bear tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Riley wanted to find her lost red sock. Grandma said, "Let's count the places we look."

"One," said Riley. She looked under the big blanket. No sock there.

"Two, three," said Grandma. They looked in two shoes by the door. No sock. "Four," said Riley. She peeked in the quiet corner by the chair. No sock.

Grandpa sang, "Five, six, seven!" They looked in the toy box, the basket, and the big pot. Still no sock.

"Eight," said Riley. She looked by the drying rack. The wet clothes were hanging there. They would dry soon.

"Nine," said Grandpa. He looked under the bed. "Ten!" he shouted. He held up the red sock.

Riley laughed. "The sock was hiding!"

Grandpa put the sock on his own ear. "Does it fit me?"

Riley giggled. "No, Grandpa! That is my sock!"

Grandma smiled and hung the sock on the rack to dry.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah went to the pool by the beach. She wanted to swim like the big kids. But when she let go of the wall, she sank down. Water went over her mouth. She grabbed the wall again.

Leah watched her teacher, Miss Jo. Miss Jo took a big breath. Then she lay flat on the water. She floated like a leaf. Leah had a question. "Do I float if I hold my breath?" "Try it," said Miss Jo.

Leah filled her lungs with air. She held it. She lay back in Miss Jo's arms. Her belly went up, up, up. Her toes came up too. She was floating! After the pool, Mom shared a crunchy apple with her. "You swam today," said Mom. Leah kicked her feet in the sand and smiled.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Hazel wanted a picnic. But her basket was empty. "I need food," she said.

She went to the kitchen. Mom cut an apple and a cheese square. Mom put in two crackers too. Hazel looked at them. "These are all foods," she said. She put the foods in her basket.

Outside, Hazel saw her toy bunny on the grass. Bunny was hungry, she thought. She gave bunny a pretend bite of apple. Then her dog Bingo ran up. Bingo made a happy sound and wagged his tail. "You are not a toy," Hazel told him. "You are an animal." She gave Bingo a real crumb. He ate it fast.

A bird flew down. It pecked at a cracker bit. Hazel laughed. Now bunny, dog and bird all sat on the blanket with her. Hazel clapped her hands. "Welcome to my picnic, friends," she said.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood still in the kitchen. "Mommy, where did the light go?" he asked.

Mommy found the big flashlight. She clicked it on. A bright beam lit up the room. "The power is out," she said. "We will use the flashlight now." She planted the flashlight on the table, standing up tall. The light shone on the wall.

Jules held his hand in the light. A big shape appeared on the wall. "Mommy, look! What is that?" he asked. "That is a shadow," she said. "Your hand is blocking the light. So the wall stays dark there." Jules wiggled his fingers. The shadow fingers wiggled too.

He made a bunny shape with two fingers up. The wall had a bunny now. He bent his fingers, and the bunny's ears flopped down. He laughed a soft little laugh.

Then Daddy came in with a small lantern. He set it on the floor. Now Jules had two shadows! One bunny on each side of him. "Two bunnies!" Jules said. He clapped his hands. Both bunnies hopped away.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Victor wanted to build a house for his toy cat. He looked for the right blocks. The square block had four flat sides. It sat still on the rug. The triangle block had three sides and pointy corners. It sat on the roof like a hat. "Good," said Victor.

But the round block would not stay up. It had no flat sides at all. Victor pushed it on top. It rolled off. It rolled right under the chair. "Oh no," said Victor. His sister Mia came in. "Let it be a ball," she said. "Cats like to chase balls." She reached under the chair and got it.

Victor gave the round block a push. It rolled across the rug. The toy cat sat next to it. The long rectangle block became the door. Victor put the cat in. Mia blew him a kiss. "Nice house," she said. Victor waved and made the cat fly out for one more roll.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Aiden finds a red book at school. The cover has a picture of a sleepy bear. Under the bear are little black marks. "Those marks say Sleepy Bear," says his teacher. Aiden lifts the cover with both hands. He turns page one, then page two, then page three. The bear yawns on each page.

Aiden wants to keep the book forever. He puts it in his cubby. He hides his coat over it. "The book lives in our book corner," his teacher says. "It is like a library book. You can take it home. Then you bring it back so other kids can read it too."

Aiden feels upset at first. He hugs the book tight. Then he sees Mia waiting. She points at the sleepy bear. Aiden looks at the marks on the cover. He opens the book for her. "Sleepy Bear," he says. Mia smiles. Aiden turns the pages, one by one, all the way to the end.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Nataly ran into the nursery. A new baby was coming today! The little crib stood by the window. It smelled like soap and clean sheets.

Natalie wanted to make the room ready. She found paper and glue. "I will make a picture," she said. She glued a big red heart onto the paper. She glued a yellow sun, too. The glue was cold and sticky on her fingers. Then she laid the blue blanket down flat in the crib. She patted it with both hands. Smooth and flat, just right for a baby.

Daddy made a road with tape on the floor. It was a long road for toy cars. "The road leads to the crib," he said. Natalie pushed a little car along the road. Vroom, vroom! The car rolled all the way to the crib and stopped.

Then they heard the door. Mommy came in. She carried a small bundle. A tiny face peeked out. "This is Baby Sam," said Mommy. Natalie touched his small hand. Baby Sam grabbed her finger and held on tight. Natalie laughed out loud. "He likes me!" she said. She taped her picture on the wall, right over the crib. Baby Sam looked up at the big red heart.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Austin waited in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to know if his ears were okay. He could not hear his mother when she whispered.

Dr. Amy smiled. She held up a little bell. She rang it near Austin's ear. Ding! Austin heard it with his ear. He turned his head. "I hear it!" he said.

Then Dr. Amy shined a tiny light. Austin saw it with his eyes. He saw the light go blink, blink. Next she held out a sticker. "Touch it," she said. Austin touched it with his fingers. It felt squishy. He sniffed a soap sample with his nose. It smelled like flowers. The nurse gave him a sweet candy. He tasted grape with his tongue.

Dr. Amy looked in Austin's ears. "Your ears are clean," she said. "I found a tiny marble in one." Austin's mother laughed. "My sock was squishy last night," she said. Austin grinned. He put the marble in his pocket. Then he rang the bell himself. Ding! His mother covered her ears. "Not too loud," she said, "or the baby will not sleep." Austin rang it very soft. Ding.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Hunter wanted warm cocoa. He wanted it fast. Mom said the milk had to heat slow on the stove. Hunter stood far back and watched. The big pot sat on the fire. The little cups waited on the table.

The sky outside turned stormy. Rain hit the window fast. A small bird sat under the big roof. It was dry there. "Smart bird," said Hunter.

The milk got hot. Mom poured it slow into Hunter's little cup. Hunter blew on it. He blew slow. Then he blew fast. The steam danced away. Mom put one cold spoon in the cup. Hunter touched the handle. The cold spoon made his cocoa cool enough for a big sip. "Mmm," said Hunter. "Cold spoon, happy tongue!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Madelyn wanted her sheep to have a house. The toy barn had four doors. One door was a circle. One was a square. One was a triangle. One was a rectangle.

She pushed the sheep to the circle door. The sheep did not fit. She pushed it to the square door. It did not fit. She pushed it to the triangle door. Still it did not fit. The old sheep had one weak leg, so it could not jump or climb. "No door fits you," Madelyn said. "No door fits you at all."

Then Madelyn saw the roof. The triangle roof sat on top. She lifted it up, up, up. The barn was open now. She set the sheep down on the soft straw. She put the triangle roof back in place.

Madelyn peeked through the little circle window. The sheep peeked back and said, "Baa."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Raphael put on his big boy shoes. He was going to school with his teacher, Miss Kim. His tummy felt jumpy and excited.

At school, a boy named Ben was crying. His block tower had fallen down. Ben looked sad. Raphael had an idea. He picked up the blocks one by one. He stacked them up tall. Then he put a red block on top. "Look, Ben," he said. "It fits!" Ben stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Now Ben looked happy.

A girl named Mia ran by too fast. She bumped the tower. Crash! It fell again. Ben's face turned red. He looked angry. "Do you want to build it again?" Raphael asked. Ben nodded. They built it together, taller than before. "Is this tower real big?" asked Raphael. "The biggest," said Ben. Miss Kim gave them each a paper star. Raphael stuck his star on his hand and waved it high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everett sat at the dinner table. He wanted the big red tomato. It sat far away, by Daddy's plate.

Everett used his eyes to look at it. It was round and shiny. He used his ears to listen. The pot went pop, pop on the stove. Daddy stirred it from far away.

"I smell it!" said Everett. His nose wiggled. "It smells like summer!"

Daddy slid the tomato closer. Everett touched it with one finger. It felt smooth and cool. But the bowl felt rough next to it.

"Try a bite," said Daddy.

Everett stuck out his tongue. He licked the tomato. He made a face. Then he froze.

"It's sour!" he said. "My tongue knows!"

Daddy laughed. Everett laughed too. He picked up the tomato with both hands. He took a big bite anyway.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Lennon wanted the red crayon. It sat on the far side of the table. Her friend Mia was using it.

"May I have the red crayon, please?" Lennon asked.

Mia smiled and gave it to her. "Thank you," Lennon said.

Then Lennon drew a big cat. She reached for the glue. The glue rolled off the table. It hit Mia's shoe and made a white spot.

"Sorry, Mia," Lennon said.

"It's okay," said Mia.

The glue bottle was too high to reach on the shelf. Lennon could not put it back. What should she do now? She walked to Teacher Rosa.

"Can you help me, please?" Lennon asked.

Teacher Rosa took the glue and put it high up. Then she picked up her phone and took a picture of the big cat.

"Wow," said Teacher Rosa. "What a spotted cat!"

Lennon looked at her cat. It had lots of spots. She started to draw another one.

"Can I have the blue crayon, please?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Cooper sat in his car seat. His cup had rolled under the seat. He could not reach it. "Help, please, Daddy," he said.

Daddy reached back and got the cup. "Here you go." Cooper took a drink. "Thank you," he said. Daddy smiled in the mirror.

Then Cooper dropped his bear. The bear sat in the middle of the floor. Cooper's foot was on the bear's paw. "Sorry, Bear," he said. He moved his foot. He hugged Bear tight.

Outside, a big truck went by. It made a loud sound. Cooper held his ears. "Will it be quiet soon?" he asked. "Yes," said Mommy. "Watch." The truck drove away. It was quiet now.

Cooper counted what he had. One cup. One bear. One blanket. "Say it again," said Mommy, and Cooper laughed and counted. One, two, three.

The car turned onto their street. Home. Cooper waved at the house. "Hello, house," he said. Daddy parked the car, and Cooper held Bear all the way to the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Gabriella went to the community kitchen with her mama. She wanted to help make bread for the family. The big mixing bowl was old and blue. Mama let Gabriella pour in the flour. It fell like soft snow. Gabriella poked the flour with one finger. "Where did my finger go?" she asked. "It is hiding in the flour," Mama said.

Next came the warm water and the yeast. Mama stirred it slow. Then they had to wait. Gabriella watched the bowl. The dough sat still, like a sleeping cat. "Is it broken?" Gabriella asked. "No, we wait," said Mama. They washed the table. They set out cups. Gabriella waited some more.

Then she looked again. The dough was big now! It had grown up and up, like a puffy cloud. Gabriella poked it softly. It squeezed back through her fingers. "It got big!" she said. Mama smiled. She put the pan into the hot oven, and Gabriella stood back.

Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Mama took out the bread with big gloves. Gabriella tore a piece for papa and a piece for grandma. She took one bite. It was soft inside. "The little dough grew into this," said Gabriella. She hugged the warm loaf, right against her cheek.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Rowan wanted a sandwich. But Mom said, "First, find the bread."

Rowan opened the bread bag. The bag was closed with a twist. He turned the twist and turned it. Then the bag opened wide.

The bread was square! "Square like my blocks," said Rowan. Mom took a big knife. She cut the bread on the diagonal. Now there were triangles! Rowan clapped. "Two triangles!"

Rowan put cheese on one triangle. The cheese was a circle. "The circle sits on the triangle," he said. Mom cut a pickle into long strips. Rectangles!

Mom sang a little song while they worked. Rowan sang too. "Square, triangle, circle, rectangle, yum, yum, yum!"

Then Rowan reached for his milk. It tipped over. "Oh no, a spill!" But Mom wiped it fast. "Mistakes are okay," she said. "Clean up, then try again."

Rowan set his cup down slowly this time. No spill at all. He bit his triangle sandwich. "Mmm," said Rowan. "Triangles taste best!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Cooper wanted his ball to roll fast. He gave it a big push. The ball zoomed across the playroom. Then he gave it a small push. The ball rolled slowly and stopped near his toe. "Hmm," said Cooper. "Big push, fast ball!"

Cooper found two cups on the little table. One cup was cold. He touched it with one finger. Brrr! Dad held the other cup. "This one is hot," said Dad. "Watch from here." Steam rose up in a curl. Cooper smelled the steam. It smelled like warm cocoa. He waited and waited. At last the hot cup turned cool too.

Then Cooper smelled something sharp. It was the orange Mom was cutting in the kitchen. She cut a big piece and a small piece. Cooper took the small piece. He chewed it slowly. Then he gave one big, happy jump. "Big jump!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Isla wanted to find her soap. It was bath time. Mama was there to help.

Isla used her eyes. She saw a yellow duck. She saw a blue pot. No soap yet.

Then Isla used her ears. She heard a drip, drip, drip. The water was running! When Mama turned the tap, the drips came. When Mama turned it off, the drips stopped. Isla clapped her hands.

Isla used her nose. She smelled something sweet. "That way!" she said. She walked to the shelf.

There was the soap. Isla touched it with her fingers. It felt smooth and slippery. She licked it with her tongue. "Yuck!" said Isla. "Soap is not for tasting." Her tummy was fine. She had only tried a tiny bit.

Mama laughed. "Good finding, Isla. Now let's wash." The water was warm and cozy. Isla rubbed the soap on her arms.

"I found it myself," said Isla. "And now the bathroom is all tidy."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Jasmine wanted a party for her bear. She looked in the toy box. She found red cups. "Red for bear," she said. She marched to the kitchen with them. "More cups, please," she said.

Mama gave her blue cups too. Jasmine set them on the floor. She found a yellow banana. "Yellow for the party," she said. She put it on a green plate. "Green plate, yellow banana. So pretty."

But bear had no hat. Jasmine looked and looked. She found a red sock. Too big. She found a blue sock. Too big. She waited. She looked again. There, under the chair, was a tiny green sock. "Green hat for bear," she said. She put it on bear's head. It fit just right.

Jasmine clapped her hands. Mama brought milk in the blue cups. Bear got the green sock hat. The banana sat on the yellow... no, the green plate. Jasmine sat down next to bear. "Now we can eat," she said. "Our party can start."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. It was snowy outside the window. The cook, Mr. Bell, set down warm toast. "Can I help?" Colton asked. "Yes," said Mr. Bell. "Spread the butter. Then pour the milk."

Colton picked up a dull little spreader. He dipped it in soft butter. He slid it across the toast. The butter made the toast shiny. "Where did the butter go?" he asked. "Into the bread," said Mr. Bell. Colton slid again. More shiny spots.

Next came the milk. Colton held the cup on the table. He tipped the pitcher a little. Milk went in, drop by drop. He tipped it too far. Milk ran over the rim. "Oh no," said Colton. He wiped it with a cloth. Then he tipped just a little. The cup filled up. Not one drop fell.

A tiny turtle sat on the shelf by the cups. Its shell was shiny, like the butter. Colton laughed. "More milk," said Mr. Bell, and slid a new cup across the table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole farmhouse went dark. Kai stood very still.

"Mama!" he called.

"I am here," said Mama. She took his hand. "The power is off. Let's find the big lamp."

Mama lit a candle on the table. The wick caught the flame. Then the little room was not dark anymore. The candle made the room glow.

Kai clapped his hands. "It works!"

"Want to help?" Mama asked. She held the candle up high. "Watch what happens when I step this way."

Mama took a step. Her shadow on the wall took a step too. It grew big, then small, then big again.

Kai giggled. He moved his arm. His shadow moved its arm!

"We are having a shadow party," said Mama.

Dada came in with blankets. They sat close on the rug. The candle flickered. The shadows danced on the wall.

"This is a pretty party," said Kai. He made a bunny with his fingers. The shadow bunny hopped.

Then the lights popped back on. The room was bright again. Kai waved at the candle.

"Bye bye, little flame," he said. "See you next time."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Julia wanted to play outside. She looked out the big window. The sun was out. It was sunny. "Hat!" said Julia. She put on her sun hat. One, two, she tapped it down.

But then the wind came. The tree bent and waved. It was windy. The wind took Julia's hat. The hat flew across the grass. Julia held her hat down with both hands. That did not work. The wind blew again.

Then rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. It was rainy. Julia ran inside. Mama gave her boots and a raincoat. Julia put them on. One boot, two boots. "Now you can splash," said Mama.

Julia splashed in a puddle. The splash made a big circle. The rain made little circles too. Julia laughed. The rain stopped. The sun came back. Julia saw something in the sky. It was a rainbow. It made a big triangle of colors over the houses.

Then soft white flakes fell. It was snowy. Julia held out her hand. One flake landed on her mitten. It was tiny and white. Mama called, "Cocoa time!" Inside, Mama held the warm cup. Julia took a sip. "Tasty," said Julia. She looked out the window at the snow. "Snow again tomorrow?" she asked.

story:
Felix loved the red truck book. Miss Dana held it up at story time. She turned the pages one by one. First page, then next, then next. The truck went beep on the last page. Felix listened to every beep.

After snack, Miss Dana said, "A librarian is coming." Felix ate his salty crackers and waited. He waited a long time. At last, a lady came with a big bag of books. Each book had little marks on the front. "Those marks are the name of the book," said Miss Dana. Felix looked close. "Truck," he said. Miss Dana smiled and nodded.

Felix picked the red truck book. "I want to keep it," he said. "It is mine now." The librarian shook her head. "You can take it home," she said. "But you need to bring it back on this day." She showed him a paper with the day on it. Felix held the book tight. Then he thought about his friend Sam. Sam liked trucks too.

"Sam can read it next," said Felix. He gave the book back on the right day. The librarian had a surprise for him. She held up another truck book. "This one is new," she said. Felix opened it, front page first, and sat down to look. "Beep," he said, turning the page.

story:
Connor sat at the dinner table. He was hungry. He wanted his favorite dinner.

"Guess what we eat tonight," said Dad. He put a bowl on the table. Connor peeked in. It was soup with carrots and noodles. Carrots were foods. Foods went in his tummy!

Connor held up his fork. "My monkey wants dinner too!" His toy monkey sat in his chair. "Monkey eats bananas," said Dad. "Bananas are foods too." Connor giggled. Monkey was a toy. Toys could not eat.

Connor gave monkey a pretend taste. Then he ate a big spoon of soup. Yum. He made a happy sound, "Mmm!" Monkey got soup on his fur.

Mom laughed. "Now monkey needs a bath." She wiped monkey's face with a napkin. Connor gave monkey a hug. Then he ate his noodles, one by one, all gone.

story:
Jordan ran to the window at daycare. Snow was falling outside. "Yesterday there was no snow," said Miss Ana. "Today the snow is here."

Jordan pressed his hands on the cold glass. The snowflakes landed one by one. Then they melted into little wet dots. Where did each flake go? Jordan watched another one land. It made a small wet dot too.

"Now we will go outside," said Miss Ana. "Later we will have warm soup." Jordan put on his boots. His boots were blue and good for snow.

Outside, Jordan found a shovel. He pushed the snow into a pile. The pile grew bigger and bigger. He patted it and made it tall. Then he tried to stack one snowball on top. The big pile held the snowball up. The tall pile did not fall down.

"When can we build more tomorrow?" Jordan asked.

"Tomorrow the snow will still be here," said Miss Ana.

Jordan looked at the tall white pile. Then he looked up at the sky. More snowflakes were coming down, one by one.

story:
Henry wanted to ride the big red swing at the park. Yesterday the swing was wet from rain, so he could not ride it. Today the sun was out, and the swing was dry. But a girl was on it now. Henry had to wait.

Henry sat on the bench with Dad. He pulled his sweater tight because the wind blew. "When is later?" Henry asked. "Soon," said Dad. They watched the clouds move across the sky. The clouds went slow, then they went fast.

Then the girl jumped off the swing. "Now it is yours," she said. Henry ran fast. Dad pushed him up high. Henry laughed. Tomorrow they would come again, and maybe the clouds would bring rain. "Tomorrow I will wear my rain boots," said Henry, kicking his feet into the blue sky.

story:
Zoey sat at the dinner table. She had a big spoon in her hand. Tonight they were having soup.

Zoey wanted to scoop the soup all by herself. She tried. The spoon went in. The soup dripped out. Plop, plop, on the table. Her face turned sad.

"Keep trying," said her father. "Go slow."

Zoey tried again. She chased a carrot around the bowl. It kept sliding away. Her face felt hot and angry. She put the spoon down.

Then the ladle slipped. A big wave of soup splashed. Zoey jumped back, scared. "It's okay," said her father. "We can wipe it up." He used a towel.

Zoey picked up her spoon once more. She held it still. She scooped slow and steady. The soup stayed on the spoon. It went into her mouth!

"I did it!" said Zoey. Her smile was big and happy. She jumped in her seat, so excited.

"Zoey scooped the soup," said her father. He clapped. Zoey clapped too. Then she chased one more carrot, and this time she caught it.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Evelyn sat at the little blue table. She was making a paper lion. First she glued on a round orange face. Then she wanted to add the mane.

Evelyn stuck on one yellow strip. It fell off. She stuck it on again. It fell off again. The strip dropped to the table.

Evelyn made a sad face. Her teacher Miss Jo came over. "Try this," said Miss Jo. She showed Evelyn how to press the strip down. "Now hold it. Count with me. One, two, three, four, five."

Evelyn pressed hard. She counted to five. Then she let go. The yellow strip stayed on! It did not fall. The glue worked when she held it first.

Evelyn clapped her hands. She took the next strip. She pressed and counted. On it went. Press and count, press and count. Soon the whole mane was on, all around the round face.

Miss Jo hung the lion on the wall. Evelyn pointed at it. "Look at my lion," she said. "I made it stay."

story:
Stella loved book day at daycare. Miss Amy put a big bag of books on the rug. "These are library books," she said. "We can borrow them and take them home. But we must bring them back by Friday, so other kids can read them too."

Stella picked a book about a red fox. She held it in her hands. The front cover had the fox on it. She opened the front first, just like Miss Amy showed. She turned the pages one by one, all the way to the back cover.

"Look at these little marks," said her friend Ben. He pointed at the page. "Those are words," said Stella. "My mom reads them out loud. They tell you what the fox says." She ran her finger under the marks. Could the marks really talk?

Stella wanted to keep the fox book forever. She hid it in her cubby. But on Friday, Miss Amy said, "Time to bring the books back." Stella marched to her cubby and got the fox book. She gave it to Miss Amy. The book went into the big bag. Another kid would read it next.

"What will you pick next time?" Miss Amy asked. Stella smiled. "Maybe a bear book," she said.

story:
Layla was building a tower with her blocks. She stacked one, two, three blocks high. "Tall!" she said. She felt so happy.

The cat jumped up. The tower fell down. Crash! Layla's lip wobbled. She felt sad. She wanted to cry.

Then the cat knocked her juice cup over too. "No, cat!" said Layla. Her face got hot. She felt angry. She stomped her little foot.

Mama came over. "Let's try again," said Mama. "The cat can watch from the chair." Mama put the cat on the soft chair. He curled up in a ball.

Layla had an idea. She would build a different tower. She made it short and wide. She put the blocks down slow, slow. She waited and patted each block.

The tower stood up. It did not fall! Layla clapped her hands. She felt excited. She jumped up and down.

The cat slept on the chair. Layla sat by her tower. She touched the top block very softly. "Stay," she whispered.

The blocks stayed still, and Layla smiled.

"Yes, that one," said Jules, pointing.

story:
Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there.

"Where is bunny?" Aubrey asked. Grandma said, "Let us look." They looked under the bed. No bunny. They looked in the toy box. No bunny. Aubrey sat down. Her lip went wobbly.

Grandma went to the window. She opened the curtain. The sun came in. It made a bright spot on the floor. Aubrey saw something. The big blanket had a lump in it. The lump was bunny-shaped!

Aubrey pulled the blanket back. There was bunny! "You were hiding!" Aubrey said. She hugged bunny tight. Grandma laughed and clapped her hands.

"Time for breakfast," said Grandma. Aubrey sat at the table. Grandma gave her milk in a blue cup. Aubrey held bunny on her lap. She let bunny take a pretend sip. "Bunny wants to share," Aubrey said. Grandma smiled. The sun made a warm spot right on bunny's soft ears.

story: Victoria was at the beach with her dad. The big pool was next to the sand. Victoria wanted to swim like the big kids. Dad held her hands in the water. "Kick your legs," he said. Victoria kicked some more. The moving water pushed her to the ladder. "I went all the way there!" she said. Dad smiled and clapped. After swimming, they walked on the sand. Victoria found a shell. Dad said, "Same time tomorrow."

story:
Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had paper, glue, and yellow paint. He wanted to make a flower for his mama.

First he had to sort his papers. He put the big ones here. He put the small ones there. Then he picked a clean white sheet for his flower.

Mohamed squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze. Squeeze. Squeeze. The glue made a big puddle on the paper. He stuck on a green stem and yellow petals. But the paper felt funny. It turned soft and wrinkly. The corner tore a little when he touched it.

"Mama, look," said Mohamed. "Too much glue."

He tried again with a new sheet. This time he made small dots. Dot. Dot. Dot. He stuck on the stem. He stuck on the petals. The paper stayed flat and clean. The flower looked bright on the white page.

Then Mohamed blinked. One petal had fallen into the paint. It came out yellow on both sides. Mama laughed and clapped her hands. Mohamed held up his flower, yellow and shiny, and turned it in the light.
